The second goal relates to reuse of content in new media, Verrone said. The agreement bases payment for reuses on a distributor's gross formula for residuals, "so that when they get paid, we get paid," he said. The third goal, which Verrone said the guild did not achieve, was to shore up writers' shares of the revenue from animation and reality television. "Giving up animation and reality was a heartbreaking thing for me personally," he said. LOS ANGELES, California (CNN) — Striking Hollywood writers will return to their keyboards Wednesday after voting overwhelmingly to end a 100-day walkout that had effectively shut down the entertainment industry.

Writers Guild of America member Steven Binder signaled his approval as he voted Tuesday in Beverly Hills, California.

More than 92 percent of Writers Guild of America members who cast ballots Tuesday in Los Angeles and New York voted to end the work stoppage over residuals for writing in the digital age, including new media and the Internet. The new agreement runs for three years.

“The strike is over. Our membership has voted, and writers can go back to work,” said Patric Verrone, president of the WGA’s West chapter.

Michael Winship, president of the WGA’s East guild, said, “The success of this strike is a significant achievement not only for ourselves but the entire creative community, now and in the future.”

WGA members walked off the job November 5 after negotiations broke down over how writers are compensated for the use of their material on the Internet, DVDs, and other platforms.

“It is not all that we hoped for, and it is not all we deserve,” Verrone said when a tentative deal was announced Saturday. But he added, “This is the best deal this guild has bargained for in 30 years.”

Leslie Moonves, chief executive officer of CBS Corp., told The Associated Press, “At the end of the day, everybody won. It was a fair deal and one that the companies can live with, and it recognizes the large contribution that writers have made to the industry.”

The Alliance of Motion Picture and Television Producers, which represents production companies and media conglomerates, has not commented on the agreement.

The vote means that the Academy Awards ceremony on February 24 will proceed as the customary scripted gala, the AP reported.

“I am ecstatic that the 80th Academy Awards presentation can now proceed full steam ahead,” without “hesitation or discomfort” for the nominees, Sid Ganis, president of the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences, which stages the Oscars, told the AP.

As long as the strike continued, the traditional Oscars spectacle remained in doubt, as many Hollywood stars would not cross WGA picket lines.

It remains unclear how soon new episodes of scripted programs will begin airing, because production cannot start until scripts are completed, the AP reported. Producers will need at least four weeks to get the first post-strike episodes of comedies back on the air, while dramas will take six to eight weeks, according to the AP.

Verrone said the WGA achieved two of its three goals through negotiations with the studios.

The first goal concerned writers’ “jurisdiction” in new media, Verrone said, meaning that any content written by guild members specifically for new media, such as the Internet or cell phones, will be covered by their contract.

The second goal involved the reuse of content in new media, he said. The agreement bases payments for reuse on a distributor’s gross formula for residuals, “so that when they get paid, we get paid,” Verrone said.

It is the “first time in our history that a new delivery system pays on a residual formula superior to the prior existing system,” he added.

The third goal, which Verrone said the guild did not achieve, was to strengthen writers’ share of revenue from animation and reality television.

“Giving up animation and reality was a heartbreaking thing for me personally,” he said. “But it was more important that we make a deal that benefited the membership, the town as a whole, that got people back to work and that solved the biggest problems in new media.”

LOS ANGELES, California (CNN) — Hollywood screenwriters are set to return to work Wednesday after voting by a wide margin to bring an end to a 100-day strike that had largely brought the entertainment business to a halt.

Writers Guild of America member Steven Binder indicated his support while casting his ballot Tuesday in Beverly Hills, California.

In voting held Tuesday in Los Angeles and New York, more than 92 percent of participating Writers Guild of America members chose to end the walkout. The dispute centered on residual payments for writers’ work in the digital era, including compensation connected to new media and the Internet. The agreement will run for three years.

“The strike is over. Our membership has voted, and writers can go back to work,” said Patric Verrone, president of the WGA West.

Michael Winship, president of the WGA East, called the outcome meaningful beyond the guild itself, saying, “The success of this strike is a significant achievement not only for ourselves but the entire creative community, now and in the future.”

WGA members began the strike on November 5 after negotiations collapsed over issues including how writers should be paid when their work is used online and on DVDs.

When a tentative agreement was revealed Saturday, Verrone acknowledged that the deal did not include everything writers had sought. “It is not all that we hoped for, and it is not all we deserve,” he said. Still, he added, “This is the best deal this guild has bargained for in 30 years.”

Leslie Moonves, chief executive officer of CBS Corp., told The Associated Press that the result was positive for all sides. “At the end of the day, everybody won,” he said. He described the agreement as fair, workable for the companies, and an acknowledgment of writers’ major role in the industry.

The Alliance of Motion Picture and Television Producers, which represents studios, production companies and major media corporations, did not comment on the agreement.

The vote also ensured that the February 24 Academy Awards ceremony could proceed as a traditional scripted event, the AP reported. Sid Ganis, president of the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences, which presents the Oscars, told the AP he was “ecstatic” that the 80th Academy Awards could move ahead “full steam ahead” and without “hesitation or discomfort” for nominees.

Had the strike continued, the usual Oscars broadcast would have remained uncertain because many Hollywood celebrities were not expected to cross WGA picket lines.

It remained unclear how quickly fresh episodes of scripted television series would return, since production could not resume until scripts were finished, the AP reported. Comedy producers were expected to need at least four weeks to get the first post-strike episodes back on television, while dramas were expected to require six to eight weeks.

Verrone said the WGA won two of its three main objectives in negotiations with the studios.

The first involved writers’ jurisdiction over new media, he said. Under the agreement, material written by guild members specifically for platforms such as the Internet or cell phones would fall under the union contract.

The second concerned payment when existing work is reused in new media. Verrone said the deal ties those residuals to a distributor’s gross formula, meaning, in his words, “so that when they get paid, we get paid.” He said it marked the first time in guild history that a new distribution method had offered residuals under a formula better than the one used for the previous system.

The third objective, which Verrone said the guild did not secure, was improving writers’ share of revenue from animation and reality television.

“Giving up animation and reality was a heartbreaking thing for me personally,” he said. “But it was more important that we make a deal that benefited the membership, the town as a whole, that got people back to work and that solved the biggest problems in new media.”

The Associated Press contributed to the report.

**Hollywood writers end 100-day strike after overwhelming vote, clearing way for TV production to resume**

*LOS ANGELES —* Hollywood writers voted overwhelmingly to end their 100-day strike, bringing to a close one of the most disruptive labor battles in the entertainment industry in two decades and allowing television productions, late-night shows and awards programs to begin returning to normal.

The Writers Guild of America announced that its members had approved ending the walkout by a margin of **3,492 to 283**, or about **92.5 percent** in favor. The vote allowed writers to return to work immediately while the guild moved separately to ratify a new three-year contract with the Alliance of Motion Picture and Television Producers, the organization representing the major studios and networks.

The strike, which began **Nov. 5, 2007**, shut down or severely disrupted a wide range of film and television work. Writers had walked off the job after negotiations broke down over compensation for content distributed through emerging digital platforms, including Internet streaming and downloads. The guild argued that the industry was shifting rapidly toward online viewing and that writers needed contract language guaranteeing payment for work reused or created for the internet. Writers also sought improved residuals from DVD sales, though the final agreement focused more heavily on new media.

At the heart of the dispute was the question of how writers would be paid as television episodes, films and original programming moved beyond traditional broadcast, cable and theatrical distribution. The WGA maintained that the studios were trying to treat online distribution as experimental, while writers feared that failing to secure terms in 2008 would lock them out of future revenue streams.

The tentative agreement reached between the WGA and producers included several key gains for writers:

- **Residual payments for ad-supported streaming** of television programs and films, after an initial promotional window.
- **Compensation for electronic sell-through**, such as permanent downloads of movies and TV episodes.
- **Guild jurisdiction over certain original content produced for new media**, particularly when budgets or distribution met negotiated thresholds.
- **Coverage for derivative new-media programming** based on existing television shows or films.
- A framework intended to give writers a share of revenue as studios expanded distribution through websites, digital stores and other online platforms.

Guild leaders described the pact as an important first step in establishing writers’ rights in the digital marketplace, though some members said the deal did not go far enough, especially on DVD residuals. Still, the large vote to end the strike reflected broad support for returning to work after more than three months of picketing.

The strike had a major effect on the television season. Late-night talk shows were among the first casualties, with many going dark soon after the walkout began. Some returned during the strike without full writing staffs, while others, including shows whose hosts had separate agreements or interim arrangements, resumed under different conditions. Scripted series were hit especially hard: many dramas and comedies ran out of completed scripts, forcing networks to halt production, shorten seasons or rely on reality programming and reruns.

With the strike over, studios and networks were expected to restart production quickly, though not all shows could return at the same pace. Multi-camera sitcoms and some half-hour comedies were expected to ramp up within days or weeks because of shorter production cycles. Hourlong dramas faced a longer turnaround, and many were expected to produce only a handful of additional episodes before the end of the spring season. Some series were unlikely to return with new episodes until the fall.

Network executives also faced decisions about which shows were worth bringing back immediately and which would be held for the next season. The strike disrupted pilot season as well, forcing studios to reconsider development schedules and potentially rely more on existing shows, reality series and previously ordered projects.

The end of the strike also eased concerns about the **Academy Awards**, scheduled for later in February 2008. The Golden Globes had already been reduced to a news-conference format because actors and writers were unwilling to cross picket lines. With writers back at work, the Oscars were expected to proceed with a more traditional ceremony.

The walkout was the WGA’s first major strike since 1988, when writers stayed off the job for 22 weeks. Although the 2007-08 strike was shorter, it came at a moment of major technological change and was widely seen as a defining confrontation over the economic future of entertainment.

For viewers, the immediate result was a gradual return of original programming rather than an instant restoration of the TV schedule. For writers, the agreement marked the beginning of formal compensation in areas that were becoming central to Hollywood’s business model. And for the studios, it ended a costly shutdown that had rippled across Southern California’s entertainment economy, affecting not only writers and producers but actors, crew members, caterers, drivers and countless workers tied to film and television production.
